notes.meaning: Four high-ranking royal officials heard what Jeremiah was saying to the people. Jeremiah was still held in the palace courtyard, but people could still come and listen to him. These princes opposed Jeremiah and wanted to silence his warnings about Babylon.

Jeremiah faithfully repeated the Lord's message to everyone who listened. Those who stayed in Jerusalem to fight would die from war, hunger, or disease, but anyone who surrendered to the Babylonians would escape with their life. The Lord had firmly decided that Babylon would capture the city, so fighting back was useless.

The officials went to King Zedekiah and demanded that Jeremiah be executed for treason. They claimed his words broke the spirit of the remaining soldiers and caused panic among the people. Instead of seeing God's merciful offer of survival, they accused the prophet of wanting to ruin the nation.

King Zedekiah gave in to the pressure and placed Jeremiah into the officials' hands. The king showed extreme weakness, admitting he could not stand up to his powerful nobles. In this cowardly moment, he sacrificed an innocent prophet just to appease his court.

The officials took Jeremiah and lowered him by ropes into an empty, muddy storage pit in the prison courtyard. The water was gone, leaving deep mire at the bottom, and Jeremiah sank down into the mud. They hoped he would quietly die there without them having to shed his blood openly.

Ebed-melech, a Cushite court official serving in the palace, learned that Jeremiah had been thrown into the pit. King Zedekiah was currently sitting at the Benjamin Gate to hear public matters and govern. Ebed-melech boldly left the royal quarters and went straight to the gate to speak to the king.

Ebed-melech openly accused the nobles of doing evil by trapping Jeremiah in the cistern. He warned that the prophet would starve to death in that dark hole, especially since the city's food supply was almost entirely gone. It was remarkable that a foreign court servant showed more justice and mercy to God's prophet than the leaders of Judah did.

The king changed his mind and ordered Ebed-melech to take thirty men to rescue Jeremiah before it was too late. Zedekiah likely assigned this large group from the guard so the princes could not block the rescue. God used the courage of an outsider to stir the king to action.

Ebed-melech went to a palace storeroom and gathered worn-out clothes and old rags. He lowered them down to Jeremiah and told him to place the cloth under his armpits so the rough ropes would not cut his skin while he was pulled up. This thoughtful kindness protected Jeremiah's weak and bruised body.

The men pulled Jeremiah up with the ropes and lifted him safely out of the miry cistern. Rather than being set completely free, he was returned to the palace courtyard where the guards were stationed. There he was kept safe from the nobles who wanted to murder him.

King Zedekiah sent for Jeremiah to meet him secretly at the third entrance connecting the palace to the temple area. The king wanted to hear a true word from the Lord about the siege. He begged the prophet not to hide anything from him.

Jeremiah hesitated, pointing out that telling the truth had repeatedly put his life in danger. He also noted that even when he gave good counsel from God, Zedekiah refused to listen. Jeremiah wanted the king to realize his own habit of ignoring God's warnings.

Zedekiah swore a private, solemn oath by the living God who gives life to all people. He promised that he would neither execute Jeremiah himself nor hand him over to the princes who wanted him dead. The king acknowledged God as the giver of breath, even while failing to fully obey Him.

Jeremiah presented God's clear choice to the king. If Zedekiah surrendered to the Babylonian generals, his life would be spared, his family would live, and Jerusalem would not be burned down. But if he stubbornly refused, the Babylonians would capture the city, burn it to ashes, and seize him as a prisoner.

Zedekiah admitted his secret fear: he was terrified of the Jewish citizens who had already deserted to the Babylonians. He worried the invaders would turn him over to these deserters to be ridiculed and mistreated. His fear of human embarrassment proved stronger than his fear of God's wrath.

Jeremiah assured the king that the Babylonians would never hand him over to the deserters. He pleaded with Zedekiah to obey the Lord's voice so that things would go well with him and his life would be spared. True safety lay in simple obedience to God's message.

Jeremiah warned that if the king refused, a worse humiliation awaited him. The royal women remaining in the palace would be captured by Babylon's officers and would sing a song of mockery against Zedekiah. They would mock him for letting his false friends lead him astray until his feet sank into ruin, just as Jeremiah had sunk into the mire.

The prophet spelled out the tragic consequences for the entire royal household. All of Zedekiah's wives and children would be dragged out to the enemy, and the king would not escape captivity. His refusal to yield would cause Jerusalem itself to be burned with fire.

Zedekiah told Jeremiah never to let the officials know what they had discussed, threatening that speaking of it could cost him his life. The king instructed him that if the princes questioned him under threat of death, he should only say he had begged not to be sent back to the harsh prison at Jonathan's house. Zedekiah remained a slave to his fear of his own court.

When the princes came and questioned Jeremiah, he told them only what the king had commanded him to say. Because no one had overheard the private meeting, the officials were satisfied and left him alone. Jeremiah kept the king's secret and stayed safe from their anger.

differ.view: Jeremiah showed human weakness by concealing the main truth instead of practicing complete openness.
Jeremiah told the truth without telling the whole truth, which was wise because murderous men had no right to the information.
Jeremiah spoke truthfully and was under no duty from God to reveal state secrets that would provoke his enemies.

notes.meaning: Jeremiah stayed in the courtyard of the guard until the day Jerusalem was captured by Babylon. God protected His prophet in the court just as He had promised. Jeremiah was still there to see the exact fulfillment of all the warnings he had delivered.
